analysis.one_liner: Lets current and former presidents, vice presidents, and federal officials move state cases into federal court and presumes they are immune.
analysis.headline: The House Judiciary Committee approved the bill 14–11 on March 21, 2025 and placed it on the House calendar; it has not received a floor vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill rewrites the federal officer removal law so that former federal officers, and current or former presidents and vice presidents, can move any state court case against them — civil or criminal — into federal court if they claim it relates to their official duties. In federal court, they would be presumed immune, and the presumption can only be overcome by clear and convincing evidence that they were not acting in their official capacity. The bill applies retroactively, including to state prosecutions already underway.
analysis.who_benefits: Current and former presidents, vice presidents, and other federal officials facing state criminal charges or civil suits. Under the bill, they could move the case to federal court, where they are presumed immune, the state's charges cannot even be considered in the immunity decision, and cases against presidents and vice presidents are dismissed unless the state proves by clear and convincing evidence that the case would not burden presidential duties. The Attorney General may represent them or pay their private lawyers with federal funds.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Current and former executive officials facing state charges

how_it_helps.text: Expands the federal officer removal statute so former federal officers and current or former presidents and vice presidents can transfer state cases to federal court by a prima facie showing that removal standards are met.

Creates a statutory presumption that federal officials are immune in removable cases, rebuttable only by clear and convincing evidence that they were not acting under color of their office — and bars courts from considering the nature or elements of the state charges when deciding immunity.
Requires automatic dismissal of cases against presidents and vice presidents unless clear and convincing evidence shows the case would not interfere with or burden their duties.
Authorizes the Attorney General to represent the official at federal expense or reimburse private counsel at a reasonable prevailing rate.

analysis.who_pays: State prosecutors and state courts lose the ability to enforce state law against executive officials, since those cases get moved to federal court or dismissed. Taxpayers bear the cost of federal legal representation for officials. And members of the public lose the ability to hold the highest executive officials accountable under state law, because immunity is presumed and the state's charges cannot be weighed in the immunity decision.
analysis.who_pays_short: State prosecutors, taxpayers, and public accountability

drawbacks.text: The immunity presumption is rebuttable only by clear and convincing evidence, and the statute bars courts from considering the nature or elements of the state charges themselves in the immunity determination — making it very hard for a state to overcome immunity even where charges are serious.
The changes apply retroactively to prosecutions and civil actions already pending when the bill becomes law, changing the rules mid-case for state prosecutions currently underway.

Cases against presidents and vice presidents must be dismissed unless the state proves by clear and convincing evidence that continuing the case would not burden their duties at all — effectively a near-automatic escape from state prosecution.
Federal taxpayers would fund the defense of officials through Attorney General representation or reimbursement of private counsel.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: There is a real argument for the bill's core idea: a federal official sued or charged by a hostile state government over official actions should be able to have the case heard in a neutral federal forum rather than a state court. This bill goes far beyond that. It presumes immunity, forbids courts from even examining the charges when deciding immunity, mandates dismissal of cases against presidents and vice presidents, and applies retroactively to pending prosecutions. Those features come at a steep cost to state-law accountability for the most powerful officials in the country, which is the very setting where accountability matters most.

outcome.mechanism: The House Judiciary Committee approved it 14–11 and put it on the House's legislative calendar, but no floor vote has happened and Congress is still in session.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on March 3, 2025 by Rep. Russell Fry (R-SC) and referred to the House Judiciary Committee.
On March 5, 2025, the committee held a markup and ordered the bill reported as amended by a vote of 14 to 11.
On March 21, 2025, the Judiciary Committee reported the amended bill (H. Rept. 119-28) and it was placed on the Union Calendar, the House calendar for bills awaiting floor action.
The bill amends the federal officer removal statute so former federal officers and current or former presidents and vice presidents can move state cases into federal court.
It establishes a presumption of immunity for federal officials in removable cases, rebuttable only by clear and convincing evidence that they were not acting under color of their office.
The changes apply retroactively to cases pending on enactment as well as cases filed afterward.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one has gained yet: the bill has not passed, so current law still governs state cases against federal officials, and the officials the bill would shield remain subject to state courts under existing rules.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Not yet determined — bill still pending

for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and is its sole sponsor.

sides.party_line_note: The committee vote was 14–11 along the majority's margin, and no Democrat has cosponsored the bill; no floor vote has occurred yet to confirm a party split.

industries.industry: Current and former presidents, vice presidents, and other executive officials
industries.note: The bill gives this group a path to move state cases into federal court, a presumption of immunity, near-automatic dismissal of cases against presidents and vice presidents, and taxpayer-funded legal defense. Its retroactivity means these protections would apply to prosecutions already underway.

State cases against executive officials would be removed to federal court or dismissed, taking away state authority to enforce state law against federal officials. Losing that authority also removes a tool of public accountability.

analysis.trajectory: The bill sits on the House calendar awaiting a floor vote. If House leadership schedules it, the party-line 14–11 committee vote suggests it would likely pass the Republican-controlled House. The Senate has taken no action on it, so the path to becoming law this session runs through the other chamber, which has not moved any version of the bill. Many bills reported to the calendar never get a floor vote.
